steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Graph neural networks (GNNs) are used widely in applications like computational chemistry, social networks and drug discovery, because they can capture complex relationships between the nodes and edges in a graph. GNNs have several graph propagation layers, and each layer updates the representation of each node by aggregating the representations of the node itself and its neighbors. But one big limitation of GNNs is the over-smoothing problem, which happens when the GNN aggregates information from the neighboring nodes again and again. Because of this the representations of nodes from different classes can become indistinguishable, and the model performance goes down.

Recent research has looked at GNNs as a discretization scheme of dynamical systems, to deal with the over-smoothing problem and also to understand GNNs better theoretically. Here each propagation layer of the GNN is a discrete step of a differential equation. These models are often called continuous-depth models, and they use memory more efficiently and can capture the dynamics of the hidden layers well.

  - new physically-inspired framework using the Kuramoto model
  - Kuramoto model: dynamics of nonlinear coupled oscillators; proxy for explaining over-smoothing
  - over-smoothing analogous to phase synchronization: all oscillators rotate with common frequency and phase
  - KuramotoGNN training scheme: balance aggregating neighbor information vs. risk of over-smoothing
  - experiments on standard benchmark datasets: beats several baselines incl. popular GNN variants on node classification
  - promising direction; new avenues for connecting GNNs and dynamical systems
- Organization
  - Sec 2 related work; Sec 3 background; Sec 4 KuramotoGNN; Sec 5 experiments; Sec 6 conclusion and future research

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Graph neural networks (GNNs) are used widely in applications like computational chemistry, social networks and drug discovery, because they can capture complex relationships between the nodes and edges in a graph. GNNs have several graph propagation layers, and each layer updates the representation of each node by aggregating the representations of the node itself and its neighbors. But one big limitation of GNNs is the over-smoothing problem, which happens when the GNN aggregates information from the neighboring nodes again and again. Because of this the representations of nodes from different classes can become indistinguishable, and the model performance goes down.

Recent research has looked at GNNs as a discretization scheme of dynamical systems, to deal with the over-smoothing problem and also to understand GNNs better theoretically. Here each propagation layer of the GNN is a discrete step of a differential equation. These models are often called continuous-depth models, and they use memory more efficiently and can capture the dynamics of the hidden layers well.

In this paper we propose a new framework, inspired by physics, for understanding GNNs and solving over-smoothing, using the Kuramoto model. The Kuramoto model describes how nonlinear coupled oscillators behave dynamically, and it is a useful proxy for explaining the over-smoothing problem in GNNs. We show that over-smoothing in GNNs is analogous to phase synchronization in coupled oscillators, where all the oscillators in the network spontaneously rotate with a common frequency and phase. Based on this we propose a new training scheme called KuramotoGNN, which encourages the model to learn representations that balance between aggregating information from the neighboring nodes and the risk of over-smoothing. In our experiments on standard benchmark datasets, KuramotoGNN does better than several baseline models, including popular GNN variants, on node classification tasks. Overall our work gives a promising direction for addressing over-smoothing in GNNs and opens new avenues to explore the connection between GNNs and dynamical systems.

The paper is organized like this. In Section 2 we give an overview of related work on GNNs. Section 3 gives background on the continuous-depth GNNs model and the Kuramoto model. In Section 4 we present our framework KuramotoGNN, together with its similarities to other continuous-depth GNN models and the over-smoothing phenomenon. Section 5 has our experimental results, and in Section 6 we conclude with a discussion of what our framework implies and directions for future research.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Graph neural networks (GNNs) have been widely adopted in applications such as computational chemistry, social networks, and drug discovery because they can capture complex relationships between nodes and edges in a graph [1,2,3]. GNNs use multiple graph propagation layers that iteratively update each node's representation by aggregating the representations of its neighbors and of the node itself. However, a significant limitation of GNNs is the over-smoothing problem, which occurs when the GNN repeatedly aggregates information from neighboring nodes. As a result, the representations of nodes from different classes can become indistinguishable, reducing model performance [4,5].

To address over-smoothing and to improve our theoretical understanding of GNNs, recent research has viewed GNNs as a discretization scheme of dynamical systems, in which each propagation layer is a discrete step of a differential equation [6,7,8,4]. Such models are often referred to as continuous-depth models; they are more memory-efficient and can effectively capture the dynamics of hidden layers.

In this paper, we propose a new physically-inspired framework for understanding GNNs and solving over-smoothing based on the Kuramoto model. The Kuramoto model describes the dynamical behavior of nonlinear coupled oscillators and provides a useful proxy for explaining over-smoothing in GNNs. Specifically, we show that over-smoothing in GNNs is analogous to phase synchronization in coupled oscillators, where all oscillators in the network spontaneously rotate with a common frequency and phase. Building on this insight, we propose a new training scheme, KuramotoGNN, which encourages the model to learn representations that balance the need to aggregate information from neighboring nodes against the risk of over-smoothing. Experiments on standard benchmark datasets show that KuramotoGNN outperforms several baseline models, including popular GNN variants, on node classification tasks. Overall, our work offers a promising direction for addressing over-smoothing in GNNs and opens new avenues for exploring the connection between GNNs and dynamical systems.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 gives an overview of related work on GNNs. Section 3 provides background on the continuous-depth GNNs model and the Kuramoto model. Section 4 presents our proposed framework KuramotoGNN, along with its similarities to other continuous-depth GNN models and the over-smoothing phenomenon. Section 5 presents our experimental results, and Section 6 concludes with a discussion of the implications of our framework and directions for future research.
